{{Short description|Swiss mathematician (1896–1936)}}
'''Gustave Juvet''' (born 25 September 1896, [[La Côte-aux-Fées]], [[Canton of Neuchâtel|Neuchâtel]] –  2 April 1936, [[Valais]]) was a Swiss mathematician.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Alunni, C.|title=Gustave Juvet (1896–1936), Un Pionnier Oublié des Études Cliffordiennes|journal=Advances in Applied Clifford Algebras|year=2009|volume=19|issue=3–4|pages=547–584|url=http://www.pensee-sciences.ens.fr/IMG/pdf/Alunni_Juvet.pdf|doi=10.1007/s00006-009-0183-2|s2cid=119919498|access-date=2016-05-16|archive-date=2017-02-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170210205810/http://www.pensee-sciences.ens.fr/IMG/pdf/Alunni_Juvet.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> He made contributions to [[relativity theory]], [[quantum mechanics]], and [[cosmology]]. He authored the first comprehensive French treatise on [[tensor calculus]] in 1922, and his work on [[Clifford algebra]]s and [[spinor]]s between 1930 and 1935 anticipated unified geometric approaches to physics that would later become influential in [[theoretical physics]].

== Biography ==
Juvet received his ''[[Licentiate (degree)|licence]]'' in mathematical sciences from the [[University of Neuchâtel]] in 1917 and then the same degree from the Sorbonne in 1919. He taught astronomy and geodesy from 1920 to 1928 at the University of Neuchâtel. In 1928 he became a professor at the [[University of Lausanne]], where he retained his academic position until his unexpected death from a heart attack in 1936. In 1926 he received his doctorate from the ''Faculté des sciences de Paris''.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Gangnebin, S.|title=Gustave Juvet 1896–1936|journal=Bulletin de la Société Neuchâteloise des Sciences Naturelles|year=1936|volume=61|url=http://www.e-periodica.ch/cntmng?var=true&pid=bsn-002:1936:61::273}}</ref>

{{blockquote|Juvet was a person of very wide interests; in mathematics, he can be characterized as a mathematical physicist interested in relativity theory, quantum mechanics, and cosmology. He had translated Hermann Weyl's ''Raum, Zeit, Materie'' (1st edition 1918) into French already in 1922 (with R. Leroy) and was a prolific author who had mastered the Levi-Civita tensor calculus fairly early in his career (in Paris).<ref>{{cite book|editor=Colbois, Bruno|editor2=Riedtmann, Christine|editor2-link= Christine Riedtmann |editor3=Schroeder, Viktor|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NGL4MBwUrYYC&pg=PA195|chapter=A Glimpse of the de Rham era by Srishti Chatterji & Manuel Ojanguren|title=Société Mathématique Suisse|publisher=European Mathematical Society|year=2010|pages=195–220|isbn=9783037190890 }} (See p. 202 for quotation.)</ref>}}

He was an Invited Speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians|ICM]] in 1928 in Bologna and in 1932 in Zürich. For the two years 1932 and 1933 he was the President of the [[Swiss Mathematical Society]].

In adolescence, while attending Neuchâtel's gymnasium, he was a close friend of [[Jean Piaget]] (who became a famous psychologist) and [[Rolin Wavre]] (who became a prominent mathematician).<ref>{{cite book|author=Vidal, Fernando|title=Piaget Before Piaget|year=1994|page=124|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6ESD-YzMyo4C&pg=PA124|isbn=9780674667167}}</ref> Juvet married in 1925.

In 1922, Juvet published ''Introduction au calcul tensoriel et au calcul différentiel absolu'', the first comprehensive French treatise on [[tensor calculus|tensor]] and [[absolute differential calculus]], establishing his reputation in the early development of relativity studies in France. From 1927 to 1928, in collaboration with [[Ferdinand Gonseth]], he advanced [[five-dimensional space|five-dimensional]] extensions of [[general relativity]] and [[electromagnetism]]—applying [[Kaluza–Klein theory]] to the metric structure of [[spacetime]] and to the [[Schrödinger equation]]. Between 1930 and 1935, he authored seminal papers on [[Clifford algebra]]s (including ''Opérateurs de Dirac et équations de Maxwell'' and works on [[spinor]]s), anticipating unified geometric approaches to physics later known as [[geometrodynamics]]. His analyses of [[Foundations of geometry|axiomatic geometry]] and structural methods in [[Theoretical physics|modern physical theories]] were cited by [[Gaston Bachelard]] and [[Albert Lautman]], reflecting Juvet's influence on the philosophical foundations of twentieth-century science.<ref name="Alunni 2002"/>
